title: What twins reveal about the future of human cloning | Nancy Segal | TEDxManhattanBeach
description:
When Dolly the cloned sheep captured the world’s attention, fear quickly overshadowed scientific understanding. Drawing on decades of groundbreaking twin research, Nancy Segal explains why identical twins offer our best real-world model for understanding the realities—and misconceptions—of human reproductive cloning. This talk replaces hype with evidence, showing how identity, autonomy, and family relationships can thrive even in the face of emerging reproductive technologies. #twins #cloning #reproduction Dr. Nancy L. Segal is a leading authority on twin research, using the science of twins to explore the foundations of human identity, genetics, and connection. She is a Psychology Professor and Director of the Twin Studies Center at California State University, Fullerton.

Her landmark work on the Minnesota Twin Study, chronicled in Born Together–Reared Apart, revealed striking similarities among twins separated at birth and earned the American Psychological Association’s William James Book Award, reshaping how we understand nature and nurture.

Dr. Segal’s work also captures powerful human stories, including Deliberately Divided, which inspired a BBC film, The Twin Children of the Holocaust, and Gay Fathers, Twin Sons. Her latest research on Colombian twins switched at birth is featured in the Netflix documentary The Accidental Twins. With nine books, over 300 articles, and the James Shields Award for Lifetime Achievement, Dr. Segal continues to illuminate what makes us who we are. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

title: Syria's only female minister: 'I'm not here for window dressing' | BBC News
description:
"On the first day, I asked 'why are there no more women?'," Hind Kabawat told the BBC's Lyse Doucet.

Kabawat is Syria's minister for social affairs and labour - the only female minister in the transitional government tasked with navigating the country's jagged road from war to peace.

Sectarian violence, which has killed thousands of people, has marred its first months in power and many of Syria's minority communities have blamed government forces.

Once an opposition leader in exile, Kabawat acknowledged the government has made mistakes since President Ahmed al-Sharaa's rebel forces swept into the capital on 8 December 2024, ending decades of the Assad family's brutal dictatorship.

But she insisted "mistakes happen in transition".

title: Remembering Who You Were | Kimberly Bryant | TEDxMakerere University Business School
description:
"Remember Who You Were Before They Tried to Tell You Who You Weren’t."

In fifth grade at Vollentine Elementary in Memphis, Kimberly Bryant stayed after school while other children ran home. 
She wasn’t in trouble. She was in training. Preparing for the spelling bee.

That early victory mattered; not because she won, but because someone saw her brilliance before the world tried to erase it.

Years later, as the only Black girl in a Vanderbilt engineering lecture hall, she raised her hand with earned confidence...and was ignored. 

In corporate boardrooms, she was mistaken for anyone but the project manager. Even after founding an organization that would reach over 100,000 girls globally, she would one day be pushed out of the very movement she built.

In this powerful and deeply human talk, Kimberly reframes resilience. It is not about never falling. It is about remembering who you were before someone tried to redefine you. It is about understanding that in the process of building something meaningful, you are also being built.

Kimberly Bryant is the founder of Black Girls Code, a global movement expanding access to technology education for girls of color. A former electrical engineer with over 20 years in industry leadership, she is a White House Champion of Change for Tech Inclusion and a member of the Women in Technology International Hall of Fame. Kimberly Bryant is an engineer, entrepreneur, and the founder of Black Girls Code, a global nonprofit expanding access to technology education for girls of color. A former electrical engineering leader with more than two decades in corporate America, she launched Black Girls Code to close the opportunity gap in STEM — growing it from a small workshop for six girls into an internationally recognized movement. Kimberly is a White House Champion of Change for Tech Inclusion and a globally respected advocate for equity, innovation, and inclusive leadership in technology. title: What E-Learning Really Changes | Hella Amarkhil | TEDxShar e Naw
description:
When internet connections fail, screens freeze, and classrooms disappear, learning does not end. It changes shape.
This talk challenges common assumptions about e-learning by showing how participation, ownership, and understanding can actually grow online. From quiet students finding their voices in chat boxes to collaboration across cities without physical contact, learning becomes more visible rather than weaker. The focus shifts from perfect connectivity to intentional design, short purposeful lessons, low bandwidth tools, and flexible access.
E-learning does not promise ideal conditions. It promises continuity. And sometimes, continuity is the difference between stopping and becoming something new. Hella Amarkhil is an educator and social impact leader with experience working with international organizations such as Amala and CMCAN, as well as local organizations including Veyaarh Holding Group, and grassroots initiatives focused on youth and women’s empowerment. She is the founder of Beacon of Hope, an organization dedicated to expanding access to education through e-learning and capacity-building programs.
She teaches English and provides counseling for English proficiency exams at Rumi Academy and Omid Afghanistan Educational Center. Currently pursuing a Bachelor of Business Administration (BBA), Hella is passionate about leveraging e-learning as a tool to create equitable and lasting educational opportunities. title: A New Trinity for African Development | Daniella Ddamulira | TEDxMakerere University Business School
description:
We are told to choose: development or environment. Progress or planet. Concrete or trees.

But what carries a higher cost: investing in clean systems today, or paying for broken ones for generations?

At 12 years old, Daniella Ddamulira learned that water, the most basic element of life, can become a source of shame, stress, and survival compromise. 

Years later, that early lesson evolved into a larger question: why, in an era of technological advancement, do 2.2 billion people still lack access to safe drinking water?

In this visionary talk, she introduces what she calls a new trinity: development through environment for the community. 

Grounded in lived experience and supported by innovation, Daniella shares how she and her team transformed Uganda’s abundant rainfall into a scalable, UV-powered purification solution designed to serve families vulnerable to waterborne disease.

Her message is both urgent and strategic: sustainable progress is not about slowing growth — it is about redesigning it. 

Leaders must ask better questions. Investors must demand integrated solutions. Communities must be included in decisions that shape their futures.

Daniella Ddamulira is a law student, Co-founder UV-Safisha Water Purifiers, an environmentalist, and social equity entrepreneur dedicated to advancing human rights and sustainable development. 

Her work reflects a generation unwilling to inherit broken systems without attempting to rebuild them.
 Daniella Ddamulira is a dynamic advocate shaping Uganda’s future at the intersection of law, social equity, and environmental stewardship. A law student with a global-minded vision, she leads initiatives that advance human rights, the rule of law, and inclusive opportunity for underserved communities. As an environmentalist, humanitarian, and social equity entrepreneur, Daniella turns advocacy into action, building solutions that balance justice, sustainability, and impact. She exemplifies the power of purpose-driven leadership — bridging ideas and action to create meaningful, systemic change. title: Before the Alarm Rings: Catching the Quiet Signals | Dr. Arvind Kumar | TEDxSGNS Youth
description: Serious health challenges rarely begin with drama. Dr. Arvind Kumar invites us to rethink how we interpret discomfort, change, and silence in our bodies. Through simple stories and everyday examples, he highlights how persistent yet painless symptoms are often adjusted to rather than acknowledged. His message is not about fear, but about attentiveness replacing panic with awareness and urgency with timely conversation. Because sometimes the most important signals don’t shout; they whisper and learning to listen early can change the dynamics. Dr. Arvind Kumar is a medical oncologist with over 17 years of experience in comprehensive cancer care. Trained at Medical College Kolkata, Patna Medical College, and AIIMS New Delhi, he is among the earliest specialists in medical oncology to return to Bihar after advanced training, contributing to the state’s oncology ecosystem. His clinical work spans adult and pediatric cancers, with focused engagement in head and neck, lung, hematological, and gall bladder malignancies. Alongside clinical practice, he has been involved in academic research, national conferences, and physician training. Through sustained public health initiatives and charitable efforts, his work reflects a long-term commitment to improving cancer awareness, access, and treatment outcomes in underserved communities. title: Finding Joy in the Middle of Life’s Battles | Siddhartha Choudhary | TEDxIIMCalcutta
description:
Some battles change everything not just our lives, but who we become.
In this deeply personal talk, the speaker shares the story of the hardest battle of his life: a 17-year journey that began with love, unfolded through illness, uncertainty, and fear, and ultimately reshaped how he sees life, purpose, and resilience. This is not a story about entrepreneurship or success it is a story about fighting for what truly matters.
The talk takes us back to the early years of marriage and into a sudden medical crisis that changed life overnight. What began as a routine illness revealed a life-threatening brain tumor, leading to a critical surgery, months of treatment, and years of uncertainty. In moments where fear could have taken over, it was the courage, calm, and strength of his wife that carried everyone else forward.
Through poetry, memory, and lived experience, the speaker reflects on what it means to keep walking when answers are unclear to fight without losing joy, to accept help, and to focus on the smallest steps when the problem feels overwhelming. Writing became a way to return to balance, to silence the questioning mind, and to reconnect with something deeper than logic.
The talk also reminds us that resilience is not about constant struggle. It is about knowing when to fight, when to dance, and when to simply enjoy being alive. Through a moving performance inspired by Michael Jackson, the speaker shows that perfection was never the goal presence and joy were.
This talk is a quiet but powerful reminder that life is not just about surviving our battles, but about finding meaning, magic, and gratitude within them. When we don’t give up even in the worst of times we often discover the best of miracles. iddhartha Choudhary is a Pune-based business leader with strong credentials in the agriculture/agribusiness and bio-resources sectors, educated at IIM-Ahmedabad, with prior experience in major agri/seed companies and ag-tech space, now focusing on new business growth at BiofuelCircle. title: Many thousands confirmed killed in recent Iran protests | BBC News
description:
The scale of the killings in Iran during the brutal recent crackdown on anti-government protesters is being laid bare.  One human rights group, whose estimates have proved accurate in the past, says it has verified more than 6,000 deaths.  The Human Rights Activists News Agency says it’s investigating reports of more than 17,000 other killings.    Other estimates have put the number who have died at more than 33,000. 

Evidence is emerging of the systematic killing of protesters, who took to the streets demanding the end of Iran’s theocratic regime.  Many of those who died were shot on the streets but there are reports of protesters being killed while being treated in hospital and people disappearing after being arrested at their homes. 

Some of the protesters have been telling the BBC about what they witnessed.  Parisa, a 29-year-old woman living in Tehran, said she knew at least 13 people who had been killed since the protests over economic conditions erupted in the capital on 28 December and evolved into one of the deadliest periods of anti-government unrest in the history of the Islamic Republic.  Mehdi, 24, also from Tehran, described witnessing multiple killings of protesters at close range by security forces.

The Iranian authorities have said that more than 3,100 people were killed, while claiming that most of them were security personnel or bystanders attacked by those they described as “rioters”. 

Most international news organisations, including the BBC, are barred from reporting inside Iran. But videos showing security forces firing live ammunition at crowds have been verified by the BBC.

title: Turning setbacks into strength | DaVida Anderson | TEDxWestminster
description: This talk explores how life’s disruptions—whether health challenges, career transitions, or personal losses—can become catalysts for growth. Through powerful storytelling and practical insights, Dr. DaVida Anderson shares how clarity, courage, and faith transform setbacks into setups for purpose. Dr. DaVida Anderson is redefining what it means to lead with purpose in a world that often measures success by titles alone. A college administrator, adjunct professor, nonprofit founder, and motivational speaker, she has mastered the art of weaving integrity, empowerment, and resilience into every facet of her work, proving that true impact begins from the inside out. Her journey started on the track as a Division I athlete at a Big Ten university, where she faced an unexpected diagnosis: only fifty percent lung capacity and asthma. That moment forced her to rethink strength, not just physically but mentally, which sparked a lifelong commitment to helping others discover their own power. Later, when faced with a choice between a lucrative corporate career in pharmaceuticals and her passion for education and service, DaVida chose purpose. Every pivot since then has been guided by clarity, courage, and faith. Her influence extends beyond boardrooms, classrooms, and the stage. With degrees from Purdue University, Loyola University Chicago, and the University of Iowa, plus a Mediation Certification from Northwestern University, she brings expertise in student affairs, leadership development, and crisis management. title: Nightclub fire kills 25 in Goa, India, officials say | BBC News
description:
A fire at a popular nightclub in the coastal region of Goa in India has killed 25 people, according to local officials.
 
Most of the victims are believed to be staff at the Birch by Romeo Lane nightclub, located near a popular beach. Tourists are also said to be among the dead.
 
Police believe a gas cylinder exploded in the club's kitchen, causing a blaze to rip through the venue on Saturday at midnight local time.
 
Most of the bodies were found near the kitchen "suggesting that the victims were employed at the club", said Alok Kumar, Goa's Director General of Police.
 
Goa's chief minister Pramod Sawant said "three to four" tourists had died but did not provide their ages or nationalities.

title: Nato intercepts Russian warplanes violating Estonian airspace | BBC News
description:
Three Russian warplanes that violated Estonian airspace have been intercepted by Nato, the military alliance has said.
 
Estonia's foreign ministry in Tallinn condemned the incursion as "brazen".  It said three Russian MiG-31 fighter jets entered the airspace of a Nato member "without permission and remained there for a total of 12 minutes" on Friday over the Gulf of Finland.
 
Nato spokesperson Allison Hart said the military alliance "responded immediately and intercepted the Russian aircraft", calling it "yet another example of reckless Russian behaviour and Nato's ability to respond". She gave no further details.
 
The Russian military has not publicly commented on the issue.
 
Tensions have escalated between the Nato military alliance and Russia since Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
 
They have risen in the last week, after Poland and Romania - both Nato members - said Russian drones breached their airspace.

title: British couple held for months by Taliban released from prison | BBC News
description:
A British couple who were detained for nearly eight months by the Taliban in Afghanistan have been released, an official with knowledge of the case has said.

Peter Reynolds, 80, and his wife Barbie, 76, who have lived in the country for nearly two decades, were held after being stopped while travelling home on 1 February.

The couple were freed through Qatari mediation, after they were transferred from Kabul's central prison to a larger prison during the final phase of negotiations, the official said.

A Qatari official said the couple will fly to Qatar for medical checks before travelling on to the UK, despite having a long-term home in Afghanistan's Bamiyan province.

It follows months of public lobbying by their family for their release.
Six days ago, an American woman who was detained with them and subsequently released told the BBC they were "literally dying" in prison and that "time is running out".

title: European leaders walk tightrope between backing Ukraine and keeping US on board | BBC News
description:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky met key European allies in London on Monday as he faces US pressure to reach a swift peace deal with Russia.
 
Zelensky held talks with UK Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, French President Emmanuel Macron and the German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
 
The meeting came amid US efforts to get Moscow and Kyiv to sign up - quickly - to a plan to end the war in Ukraine.
 
For Kyiv, the crucial issues are the question of ceding territory to Russia as part of any peace deal and obtaining strong security guarantees to ensure that Moscow respects an eventual agreement.
 
The big names Starmer hosted in London discussed hugely significant issues - not only for Ukraine's future, but for the security of the continent as a whole.

description:

title: Breaking the Myth: A Woman with a Tabla | Anuradha Pal | TEDxIIM Sambalpur
description:
What happens when you refuse to fit into the roles society has already decided for you?

In this powerful talk, tabla maestro Anuradha Pal shares her journey of entering a male-dominated, lineage-driven classical music world as a young girl with no musical background. From facing early scepticism to performing on global stages, she reveals how illusions about gender, tradition, and capability can be challenged through dedication and mastery.

Through her personal experiences, she introduces her framework of the three Ds—dedication, discipline, and domain knowledge—and the three Cs—commitment, creativity, and compassion. Her story is not just about music but about innovation, leadership, and the courage to redefine what is possible.

This talk reminds us that true innovation is not about creating something entirely new but about challenging the illusions that limit our potential. Anuradha Pal is a world-renowned tabla maestro, composer, and bandleader, widely recognized as one of the first professional female tabla players on the global stage. She has performed at prestigious venues and festivals across the world, including the iconic Woodstock Festival.

Breaking barriers in a traditionally male-dominated and lineage-driven field, she founded India’s first all-female classical fusion band, creating opportunities for women musicians across the country. Through her performances, workshops, and initiatives, she has mentored and empowered hundreds of artists.

Anuradha has also served as a cultural ambassador and actively supports social initiatives, including campaigns for women’s empowerment. Her journey stands as a powerful example of how dedication, discipline, and creativity can challenge long-standing illusions and redefine possibilities. description: The talk, How to Stop Failing at Forming New Habits, exposes one of the biggest myths in personal development: that habit formation is about discipline, motivation, or time. title: Huge anti-government protests across Iran | BBC News
description:
Huge crowds of protesters have been marching through Iran's capital and other cities, videos show, in what is said to be the largest show of force by opponents of the clerical establishment in years.
 
The demonstrations in Tehran and the second city of Mashhad on Thursday evening were not dispersed by security forces.
 
It was the 12th consecutive day of unrest that has been sparked by anger over the collapse of the Iranian currency and has spread to more than 100 cities and towns across all 31 of Iran's provinces, according to human rights groups.
 
The US-based Human Rights Activist News Agency said at least 34 protesters - five of them children - and eight security personnel have been killed, and that 2,270 other protesters have been arrested.
 
Norway-based monitor Iran Human Rights said at least 45 protesters, including eight children, have been killed by security forces.

BBC Persian has confirmed the deaths and identities of 22 people, while Iranian authorities have reported the deaths of six security personnel.

description:
The suspected gunmen in the Bondi Beach attack threw explosives at the start of the deadly incident and had practised shooting weeks before, according to new court documents.
 
They allege the pair "meticulously" planned the attack for several months and, two days prior to the shooting, visited Bondi for reconnaissance.
 
Fifteen people were killed and dozens more injured when two gunmen opened fire on a Hanukkah celebration on 14 December. Explosives, including a "tennis ball bomb", failed to detonate, according to the documents.
 
Naveed Akram, 24, has been charged with 59 offences, including 15 counts of murder and one of terror. A second gunman - his father, Sajid Akram - was shot dead by police at the scene.

title: Leading From The Back | Rajesh Srivastava | TEDxBHIS Kanpur Youth
description:
An Innovative Style of Leadership in Aa AI Powered World

For nearly 200 years, the world has been led by a single dominant model of leadership—Leading from the Front.
This model emerged during the Industrial Revolution, when mass production outpaced local markets. To address this challenge, industrial revolution pioneers turned to two powerful institutions for inspiration—the Church and the Military—and chose the military.
The military offered a clear template—an all-knowing, all-powerful General, supported by a rigid command-and-control structure, which ensured that orders issued were obeyed. Corporations mirrored this model, with the CEO replacing the General.
For generations, this model worked effectively—until Industry 4.0 (IR4) arrived. Powered by AI, it triggered three tectonic shifts:
• An explosion and democratization of data, making it impossible for any one person to “know it all”
• Unprecedented uncertainty, volatility, and disruption, rendering rigid command & control structure ineffective.
• The entry of Gen Z—and soon Gen Alpha—who abhor command & control driven leadership & structure.
The old model of Leading from the Front is broken. It is no longer equal to the demands of an AI-powered world.
This TEDx Talk introduces an innovative style of leadership: Leading from the Back.
‘Leading From The Back’ replaces the myth of the all-knowing boss with distributed leadership—leaders at every level. It creates empowered teams, intrinsically motivated to pursue bold goals and achieve them, while freeing senior leaders to focus on long-term strategy and future readiness.
Empirical research shows that organizations embracing this style:
• Improve their chances of successfully adopting AI
• Attracting and retaining talent, especially Gen Z and the soon to come Gen Alpha
And perhaps most importantly, leaders who lead from the back gain something invaluable—time: time for health, well-being, and spend meaningful time with family.
It is time to say au revoir to Leading from the Front and embrace Leading from the Back—to not just survive, but thrive, in an AI-powered world that is already upon us.

 Rajesh Srivastava is a seasoned business leader, bestselling author, mentor, and corporate coach with decades of experience driving innovation across organisations. He has served as CEO of JK Helene Curtis, and his insights into leadership, strategy, and customer-centric growth have made him a respected voice in management circles. Rajesh is the author of The New Rules of Business and The 10 New Life Changing Skills, both published by Penguin Random House and recognised nationally; his work has also been translated into Korean, reflecting international appeal. No deaths have been confirmed in Jamaica so far but 20 people, including 10 children, are reported to have died in flooding in Haiti.
 
The UK government has now deployed urgent hurricane relief to the Caribbean.

title: US pursuing third oil tanker off Venezuela as military build-up continues | BBC News
description:
The United States Coast Guard is in "active pursuit" of an oil tanker sailing in international waters off the coast of Venezuela, according to US officials.   It follows the seizure of two other tankers by the US in recent days. 

US President Donald Trump has ordered a "blockade" of sanctioned oil tankers entering and leaving the country, accusing Venezuela of using oil revenue to fund drug-related crime and terrorism.

A US official said the latest ship being targeted was part of a "sanctioned dark fleet that is part of Venezuela's illegal sanctions evasion” and said it is “flying a false flag and under a judicial seizure order."

Venezuela has described the seizures as theft, kidnapping and piracy and accuses the Trump administration of seeking to overthrow its president Nicolas Maduro. 

In recent weeks the US has been building up its military presence in the Caribbean Sea, with growing speculation that the Trump administration could launch a direct military attack on Venezuela.   

The US has also been carrying out a series of air strikes on boats it accuses of smuggling drugs from Venezuela, killing around 100 people.

title: The Music Inside Life’s Chaos | Sudipto Das | TEDxNITKSurathkal
description:
Many times, we think of chaos as disorder or restlessness, something that should either be avoided or shunned. However, what if chaos is actually the very meaning of life? In this TEDx talk, Sudipto examines the idea of restlessness as evidence of being alive. He draws connections between art, science, and philosophy, starting with the poetry of Javed Akhtar, the scientific discoveries of Nikola Tesla, the wisdom of Kabir, and the teachings found within the Bhagavad Gita.
Through a series of powerful metaphors and true accounts, such as the use of Mahatma Gandhi's principles of non-violence and the bravery demonstrated by the employees of the Taj Hotel during the November 26, 2008, terrorist attacks, this talk shows how the ability to visualize allows us to find the truth within the chaos that surrounds us. The speaker also highlights that seeking chaos is not a way to welcome the disorder. Instead, it enables us to discover and build a framework for three key criteria for excellence, which are fearlessness, selflessness, and a commitment to perfection rather than results. Once these three qualities have developed, they often result in the creation of excellence, such as a nation rebuilt, a scientific breakthrough, a piece of music that inspires, or a righteous battle won.
 Sudipto Das is an author, musician, tech leader, and social thinker. He is an alumnus of IIT Kharagpur and co-founder of two startups. He is known for his novels, “The Ekkos Clan” and “The Aryabhata Clan”. He is also a trained violinist and composer whose work blends history, culture, and art to explore the deeper harmonies of human experience. title: BBC confronts man bulk-buying and reselling UK driving tests  | BBC News
description:
Driving instructors are being offered kickbacks of up to £250 a month to sell their official test-booking login details to touts, a BBC investigation has found.
 
Touts use these login details to book driving tests in bulk and sell them to learners on WhatsApp and Facebook, charging as much as £500 for tests that should cost no more than £75. 
 
This makes it harder for learners to book through legitimate routes and adds to already lengthy waiting times.
 
The BBC confronted Anil Ahmed, who buys driving instructors' login details and then sells tests online at a mark-up. He says the claims we put to him are a "complete fabrication".
 
Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander recently announced plans to change driving test rules, which it is hoped will stop touts and reduce the backlog. Only learners - not instructors - will be able to book test slots from spring 2026.

title: Ugly Truth About the World’s Most Expensive Skyscrapers
description:
The world’s most expensive skyscrapers look like symbols of ultimate success, but the ugly truth is that behind the glittering glass and jaw-dropping prices, they come with huge costs that almost nobody talks about. Some of these skyscrapers cost more than entire small countries spend on health or education in a year, and the money poured into them often stays out of reach for everyday citizens while elite investors benefit the most. Building at insane heights requires materials and engineering that push human limits, and that means delays, cost overruns, dangerous working conditions, and environmental damage just to get them standing. Once they’re open, huge portions of their space sit empty because only a tiny number of ultra-rich tenants can afford to rent or buy there, turning them into giant, shiny monuments to inequality.

Dr. Kaydian Simone Reid is an Associate Professor and Director of Public Health Programs at the University of Saint Joseph, where her research, teaching, and practice focus on health equity. As a mixed-methods researcher, she explores how ethnic identity affects the health of English-speaking Afro- Caribbean immigrants, examining its role in shaping health practices and outcomes across generations. Her academic work is rooted in real-world public health experience
and personal insight as an Afro- Caribbean immigrant woman. Being both an immigrant and a mother, Dr. Reid brings personal and professional dedication to her field. Her notable achievements include the 2022 Dean’s Excellence in Teaching Award and the 2023 Reverend Stack Teaching Excellence Award—the university's highest teaching honor—as well as a 40 Under Forty community service award. Dr. Reid’s career is devoted to understanding and improving sustainable community and population health through research, teaching, mentorship, service, and practice. title: Something Deep Underground Is Changing Our Planet Right Now
description:

Some of these signals point to processes happening far below our feet, like mantle movement, melting ice redistributing weight, or changes in Earth’s interior structure. We break down what scientists expected to see versus what actually showed up in the data, without getting lost in heavy physics. It’s one of those moments where Earth reminds us it’s still very much alive — and doing things we’re only just starting to notice 🌍

title: Jaguar Land Rover extends shutdown after cyber-attack | BBC News
description:
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) has confirmed that production in its factories will remain suspended until next month at the earliest, as it continues to deal with the fallout from a cyber-attack in August.
 
The UK business secretary and industry minister are visiting the West Midlands for the first time since the cyber-attack to meet JLR and firms in its supply chain.
 
The company has been unable to produce cars since the attack at the end of August forced it to shut down its IT networks, and fears are growing that some of its suppliers could go bust without support.
 
JLR has confirmed that its factories - including its UK facilities in Solihull, Halewood and Wolverhampton - won't resume operations until at least 1 October.

Mr Mahendra Luniya works in the field of digital gold and financial systems, with long term experience in the Indian gold ecosystem. His work focuses on understanding how gold is stored, traded, and integrated into modern financial practices, particularly through digital and structured formats.

Over the years, he has been involved in initiatives related to gold deposits, digital gold mechanisms, and alternative ways of engaging with gold as an asset. His interest lies in exploring how traditional forms of wealth can interact with evolving financial technologies and regulatory frameworks.

Mr Luniya has participated in public discussions and media conversations on topics related to gold, finance, and economic behavior. title: ‘Flowercycling’ technologies to reduce the pollution | Ankit Agarwal | TEDxBHIS Kanpur Youth
description:
Every year, more than 8 Million Metric tons of pesticide-laden temple-flowers are dumped in the Ganges, choking the river & causing severe health concerns - diarrhea, hepatitis & cholera. At Phool.co, over 11.4 tons of temple-waste is collected daily in Uttar Pradesh & Bihar and converted into charcoal-free incense and an animal-free alternate to leather called Fleather (PETA’s Best Innovation in the Vegan World 2020). In the process, Phool.co employs women who were previously manualas scavengers, to sort the flower waste and hand roll the popular incense sticks. This transformational disease-free employment enables these women to shun lives in which they jump neck deep into clogged sewers & scrape human faces from dry toilets. Awarded the Fast company world changing ideas and recognized by Forbes, Fortune, Business Insider and Stanford Social Review, Phool.co is driving systems change in a community that has been exploited for centuries by creating opportunities & revolutionizing the way India handles the ‘Million-ton temple waste disposal'.
 Ankit Agarwal is a social entrepreneur and founder of Phool.co, an award-winning biomaterials and sustainability venture that transforms floral waste into eco-friendly products, including charcoal-free incense and vegan “fleather.” From Kanpur, India, Ankit has built Phool into a widely recognized example of circular innovation, creating dignified employment opportunities and reducing environmental pollution. His work has earned recognition from Forbes 30 Under 30 and the United Nations Young Leader for SDGs Award, and has been featured by global platforms including Stanford and international sustainability networks. title: Social media firms face landmark trial in US | BBC News
description:
A landmark social media addiction trial in which top tech executives are expected to testify begins on Tuesday in California.
 
The plaintiff, a 19-year-old woman identified by the initials KGM, alleges the design of the platforms' algorithms left her addicted to social media and negatively affected her mental health.
 
The defendants include Meta - which owns Instagram and Facebook - TikTok's owner ByteDance and YouTube parent Google. Snapchat settled their case with the plaintiff last week. 
 
The closely-watched case at Los Angeles Superior Court is the first in a wave of such lawsuits, which could challenge a legal theory used by tech firms to shield themselves from culpability in the US.
 
Meta says it has introduced dozens of tools to support a safer environment for teens online, and the companies are expected to argue any asserted harms are caused by third-party users.

title: Swiss fire horror - claims fireworks set ceiling ablaze - around 40 dead and 115 injured | BBC News
description:
Around 40 people are  known to have been killed and 115 injured in the fire that tore through a packed Swiss bar filled with New Year revellers.   The blaze began at around 0130 local time at Le Constellation bar in Crans-Montana, high in the Alps in south-west Switzerland.  The region is a tourist and skiing destination popular with visitors from across Europe and beyond. 

60 survivors are being treated in hospital in the nearby town of Sion.  Others have been transferred to hospitals in other Swiss cities and neighbouring countries. A doctor at Geneva University Hospitals said patients are suffering from severe burns and the effects of breathing in smoke.  He said many of the patients were "very young... between 15 and 25 years old".  A significant number of those injured are in a critical condition

Some witnesses have said celebration candles or flares carried on top of champagne bottles set fire to the ceiling, starting the blaze.  Videos show fire spreading quickly across the bar’s dimly-lit ceiling.  However the Swiss Attorney General Beatrice Pilloud said the cause of the blaze was not yet confirmed.  She said teams were working to establish answers as quickly as possible.  The authorities have ruled out a deliberate attack. 

Neighbouring countries Italy and France - as well as the European Union - are providing medical support including the use of hospital burns units.  The French foreign ministry has said eight of its citizens are missing following the fire.   Three Italian citizens have been transferred to hospital in Milan while two others in critical condition are being treated in Switzerland. 

Survivors have been describing desperate scenes as people trapped inside the building tried to escape the inferno.   One man described how he managed to break a window and escape with much of his clothing burned away. 

The Swiss President Guy Parmelin said the fire was “one of the worst tragedies that our country has experienced”.

title: Why Teen Authors Should Publish NOW | Rohan Dhulipalla | TEDxMoorestown Friends School
description: In this TEDx talk, Rohan Dhulipalla challenges the advice most young writers hear when they want to publish a book: wait until you are older. He traces his journey from writing his first book as a child to being told at eleven that his ideas were not ready yet, and argues that stories have an expiration date. Drawing outside cultural examples from other creative industries, namely music and media, Rohan shows that adolescence is not a warm-up period for creativity but one of its most powerful stages, marked by higher authenticity and flexibility. Pushing to wait and “develop” does not strengthen nor protect young voices, it dulls them. Rohan Dhulipalla is a junior at Moorestown Friends School. Outside of his classes, he is the founder of Teenuscript, a publishing house run by and for teen authors, the executive editor at several literary magazines and also a TikToker in his free time. His talk will explore the future of publishing as traditional models grow outdated, highlighting how technology, community, and risk-taking can reimagine the industry. He will focus on how young (or, really any age) writers can fit and position themselves in this shifting landscape, raising the broader question of what it means, and what it costs, to “wait” in creative industries. description:
US President Donald Trump has said he "didn't see" the part of a social media video which showed a racist clip depicting Barack and Michelle Obama as apes.
 
The clip - set to the song The Lion Sleeps Tonight - was at the end of a 62-second video he shared containing claims about voter fraud in the 2020 presidential election. The video was later removed.
 
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Trump said "I didn't make a mistake" when asked whether he was going to apologise.
 
He added he had only seen the beginning of the video before it was posted by a staff member and didn't know it contained that depiction of the Obamas.

title: Uganda bus crash leaves more than 40 dead | BBC News
description:
Forty-six people have been killed after several vehicles crashed on a major highway in Uganda, the police say.
 
The police revised down an earlier death toll of 63, saying they had mistakenly included victims who were unconscious and were now being treated.
 
The crash occurred when two buses travelling in opposite directions "met head on" while trying to overtake two other vehicles – a lorry and a car – on the Kampala-Gulu Highway, the Uganda Police Force said.
 
One of the buses swerved in an attempt to avoid a crash, but in the process caused a "head on and side collision" that led to a "chain reaction" in which other vehicles lost control and overturned.

title: Manufacturing With BIM: The Cubicle Centre Story | by The B1M
description:
Manufacturing With BIM: The Cubicle Centre Story, by The B1M. An incredible case study on BIM for manufacturers.
For more BIM videos subscribe now - http://ow.ly/GxW7y 

“Some people think a cubicle is just a cubicle, but we take our business seriously” says Craig Sewell, stirring our hot coffees on a freezing morning in West Yorkshire, UK. “I started here straight out of University and thought: toilet cubicles, really? I’ll do it for a summer to pay the bills”. 

It’s now 10 years later, and Craig is Brand and Marketing Director.

As The B1M team standing on the other side of the small kitchen, we’re reassured by his candour. Thankfully it’s not just us that feel this is a little unusual.

Cubicle Centre have come a long way since 1997 when founder David Thorpe made his first unit by hand in a Dewsbury garage. Formed as a business in 1999, they now employ 25 people and turnover £4M a year. They supplied 2,500 toilet cubicles to the London 2012 Olympic Village and recently became the first cubicle manufacturer in the UK to invest in BIM. 

And that is what has brought us here. 

Our ambition is to create an engaging documentary about BIM and toilet cubicle manufacturing. We know that sounds amusing. We know it won’t win an Oscar. But bear with us a moment, and look a little deeper. 

Cubicle Centre’s BIM journey is an inspirational story locked inside modest people. They’re doing a great job but don’t really realise it. What we shine a light on here is people – normal people like you and I – seeing real benefits to their business and working lives as a direct result of using BIM. 
 
This documentary uncovers the pure honesty of their motives: “BIM was about improving ourselves first and foremost” explains Craig. “It has enabled us to improve lead times and increase productivity, so it was a no-brainer really”. 

They’re now projecting a five working week saving as a result of streamlining the design-to-manufacture process. Having created 3D components of their products with specification and attribute data attached, project teams can accurately model, specify and cost washroom spaces. Cubicle Centre then simply generate works orders and cutting lists directly from the Project Information Model. The process is both quicker and more accurate than before. 

Could you imagine an extra five working weeks in your own financial year?

If you think the finished film and its participants look highly polished and better than anything you or your team could do, then take a couple of minutes to watch the bloopers video (http://www.theb1m.com/video/b1m-bloopers-cubicle-centre). We interviewed real people in this documentary – not actors – and all they did was speak from the heart. Putting a strong edit together is our part. 

Our ambition at The B1M has always been to take BIM to a wider audience with free and engaging video content. So we’re proud to release our first BIM documentary. We want it to showcase Cubicle Centre’s work and inspire others around the world…. enjoy!

title: Donald Trump's tariffs questioned in high stakes Supreme Court hearing | BBC News
description:
Donald Trump's sweeping use of tariffs in the first nine months of his second term was sharply questioned during oral arguments before the Supreme Court on Wednesday.
 
Chief Justice John Roberts, and justices Amy Coney Barrett and Neil Gorsuch – three conservative jurists considered swing votes in this case - peppered US Solicitor General John Sauer, representing the president's administration, during his more than 45 minutes before the court.
 
"The justification is being used for power to impose tariffs on any product from any country in any amount, for any length of time," Roberts said.
 
If the court ruled for Trump in this case, Gorsuch wondered: "What would prohibit Congress from just abdicating all responsibility to regulate foreign commerce?"
 
He added that he was "struggling" to find a reason to buy Sauer's arguments.
 
The case centres around a 1977 law, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), that Trump's lawyers have said gives the president the power to impose tariffs. Although the Constitution specifically vests Congress with tariff authority, Trump has claimed that the legislature delegated "emergency" authority to him to bypass longer, established processes.

title: Staying Human in a World That Moves Too Fast | Drashtant Varma | TEDxUNB
description:
In his talk, “Staying Human in a World That Moves Too Fast,” Drashtant discussed his experiences in student leadership, government, and politics. With the hopes that we can all reflect on a commitment to amplifying voices, driving meaningful change, and engaging communities with purpose. Through all his experiences, he's learned three very simple things: His inner child keeps him grounded; There’s a lot young leaders aren’t told; And politics and life move fast. 
But it serves us well to stay grounded in what reminds us that we're human. And to never stop seeing the people behind everything, because leadership with humanity is just management. 
With personal anecdotes, Drashtant highlights that most things that seem like the end of the world aren't. And to laugh when you can, enjoy what you do - and if you need to, touch some grass. And to always remember the part of us that doesn't move fast, even if the rest of the world does. Drashtant is a fourth-year Business student at the University of New Brunswick, majoring in Economics, with plans to pursue law school. With a deep interest in law, politics, government, and public policy, he is driven by the idea that meaningful change happens when these worlds connect.
 
Originally from Gujarat, India, he immigrated to Canada with his family in 2006 and has called Fredericton home ever since. Over the years, he has been deeply involved in his community through student governance and municipal, provincial, and federal politics, often finding himself as the youngest person in the room. Those experiences have shaped not only his leadership but his perspective on growth, pressure, and what it means to stay grounded in fast-moving spaces. title: Boy with rare condition amazes doctors after world-first gene therapy | BBC News
description:
Three-year-old Oliver Chu has astounded doctors with his progress after becoming the first person in the world with his devastating disease to receive a ground-breaking gene therapy.
 
"Every time we talk about it, I want to cry because it's just so amazing," says the boy’s mother, Jingru.
 
He has a rare, inherited condition called Hunter syndrome - or MPSII - which causes progressive damage to the body and brain.
 
In the most severe cases, patients with the disease usually die before the age of 20. The effects are sometimes described as a type of childhood dementia.
 
Due to a faulty gene, before the treatment Oliver was unable to produce an enzyme crucial for keeping cells healthy.
 
In a world first, medical staff in Manchester, UK, have tried to halt the disease by altering Oliver's cells using gene therapy. Now, a year after starting treatment - he appears to be developing normally.

title: Trump makes unproven link between autism and Tylenol | BBC News
description:
Donald Trump has urged pregnant women not to take the painkiller paracetamol - known as Tylenol in the US - because of an unproven link to autism.
 
The US president said that doctors will soon be advised not to prescribe it, and that pregnant women should "fight like hell" to only take it in cases of extreme fever.
 
Medical experts have strongly pushed back on the claims, with some calling the president's comments dangerous.
 
The American College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists disputed the link made by Trump in the Oval Office, saying the claim "is not backed by the full body of scientific evidence and dangerously simplifies the many and complex causes of neurologic challenges in children".
 
Health officials in the UK have stressed that paracetamol remains the safest painkiller available to pregnant women.

title: How founders beat loneliness | Marina Davidova | TEDxWoodLaneWomen
description:
In this deeply moving TEDx talk, Marina Davidova confronts the silent epidemic hiding behind startup culture — loneliness.
With 16 years in venture capital and experience backing over 150 companies, Marina reveals what most founders won't say out loud: 76% feel lonely, and the rest are too busy pretending they're not. Behind the pitch decks and polished confidence lies a world of masks — performed for investors, customers, and teams — where real human connection quietly disappears.
Through her own raw story of betrayal, immigration, and rebuilding during COVID, Marina shares how losing trust in partnerships, friendships, and herself led her to a powerful realisation: control is an illusion, but we do have agency over the inputs that shape our lives.
She introduces her Triple B framework , a personal operating system for resilience:
1. Body – Scheduled recovery, movement, and letting the body carry pain away.
2. Brain – Feeding the mind through learning, curiosity, and growth.
3. Belonging – Gathering with people you don't have to perform for
But Marina doesn't stop at the personal. She shows how these principles can be engineered into communities, designing for psychological safety, trust, and repeated cooperation. Her own venture capital firm, built as a tribe of 400 people, is living proof: 94% of members say helping others is valued, and 75% feel safe to ask for help without judgement.
Her message is clear: the most valuable thing you can build isn't a unicorn company, it's a community where no one has to walk alone.
If you've ever worn the mask, carried the weight, or pretended everything was fine, this talk will light something in you. Marina Davidova is co-founder and Managing Partner of DVC, a community-powered fund backed by over 160 founders and engineers from leading AI companies like OpenAI, Google, Meta, Tesla, and Microsoft. DVC leverages collective expertise and in-house AI workflows to source deals and support its portfolio, including the AI-search deacon Perplexity AI, a breakthrough AI chipmaker Etched, and Mira Murati’s Thinking Machines Lab. Marina’s hands-on leadership oversees DVC’s strategy, investment process, and community. title: Ukraine reaches “understanding” with US on peace plan as Trump says “deal may be close” | BBC News
description:
Ukraine says a "common understanding" has been reached with the US on  a peace deal aimed at ending the war with Russia.

The proposal is based on a 28-point plan presented to Ukraine by the US last week.

In a post on social media, US President Donald Trump said the original plan had been fine-tuned and “a deal may be close”.   He’s sending his special envoy Steve Witkoff to Moscow discuss the plan with Russia’s President Putin.

The Kremlin said earlier that Russia had not yet been consulted on the new draft deal and warned that it might not accept amendments to the original plan.

Some of the key issues which divide Russia and Ukraine are reported to remain unaddressed so far – including security guarantees for Ukraine and control of several regions in the east of the country.

European leaders have expressed scepticism that peace could be in reach.  The French President Emmanuel Macron said he saw "no Russian will for a ceasefire" while the UK warned there was still “a long way to go."

Clive Myrie presents BBC News at Ten reporting by James Waterhouse in Kyiv,  Steve Rosenberg in Moscow and Sarah Smith in Washington.

title: Keir Starmer tells Roman Abramovich to 'pay up now' or face court | BBC News
description:
The UK prime minister has said Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich must "pay up now" to victims of the war in Ukraine or face court action.
 
Mr Abramovich, the former owner of Chelsea Football Club, pledged in 2022 that the £2.5bn he made from the sale of the club would be used to benefit victims of the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
 
But there has been a delay in releasing the funds, which are currently frozen in a British bank account, due to a standoff over how exactly they should be used.
 
Sir Keir Starmer told the Commons on Wednesday: "My message to Abramovich is clear: the clock is ticking."
 
The government wants the money to be used for humanitarian aid, but Mr Abramovich insisted it should be used for "all victims of the war" – meaning that Russians could also benefit.
 
Mr Abramovich's representatives declined to comment.

title: Row between India and China after air passenger detained | Global News Podcast
description:
The detention of Pema Wangjom Thongdok, an Indian citizen living in the UK, at Shanghai airport has fuelled a diplomatic spat between Delhi and Beijing.

The passenger said she was detained by immigration officials while travelling from London to Japan via Shanghai last Friday because her passport lists her birthplace as the northeastern Indian state of Arunachal Pradesh.

China disputes India's control of the region and considers Arunachal its territory, calling it "South Tibet" - a claim India firmly rejects.

BBC South Asia specialist Anbarasan Ethirajan has been telling the Global News Podcast more about the history of  Arunachal Pradesh and why it is such a sensitive issue in the region.

title: Zelensky ready to join Trump-Putin talks after ‘frank’ White House meeting | BBC News
description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said he would be ready to join Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin at a proposed summit in Hungary if he were invited.

The US and Russian presidents announced on Thursday they planned to hold talks on the war in Ukraine in Budapest, possibly in the coming weeks.

In comments released on Monday, Zelensky told reporters: "If it is an invitation in a format where we meet as three or, as it's called, shuttle diplomacy… then in one format or another, we will agree.”

description:

title: UK net migration down 80% from its peak in 2023 | BBC News
description:
Net migration to the UK fell by two-thirds in the year ending June 2025 compared with the previous 12 months, provisional figures indicate.
 
The difference between the number of people arriving in the country and those leaving was 204,000, down from 649,000, with the fall mainly driven by fewer arrivals for work and study reasons, the Office for National Statistics said.
 
It comes as Home Office figures show the number of people who claimed asylum in the year to September 2025 reached a record high of 110,051.
 
The figures also show the number of asylum seekers in hotels as of September rose by 2% compared with the same time last year.

title: Voyager Found Something Terrifying at the Edge of the Solar System
description:
Voyager spacecraft flew farther than anything humans ever built and ran into something scientists didn’t expect at all. At the edge of the solar system, instruments detected a strange boundary that acts almost like a cosmic wall. This region blocks and deflects particles in a way that feels unsettling, like the solar system hitting an invisible barrier. Researchers say it marks where the Sun’s influence finally loses its grip to interstellar space. And in this video, we’ll break down what Voyager found, what this “wall” really is, and why it sounds way scarier than it actually should be.

title: Russian fighter jets violating Estonian airspace intercepted by Nato | BBC News
description:
Three Russian warplanes that violated Estonian airspace have been intercepted by Nato, the military alliance has said.
 
Estonia's foreign ministry condemned the incursion as "brazen". 
 
It said three Russian MiG-31 fighter jets entered the airspace of a Nato member "without permission and remained there for a total of 12 minutes" on Friday over the Gulf of Finland.
 
Nato spokesperson Allison Hart said the military alliance "responded immediately and intercepted the Russian aircraft", and called it "yet another example of reckless Russian behaviour and Nato's ability to respond".
 
The Russian military has not publicly commented on the issue.

title: Connecting with beauty and wellbeing at a deeper level | Dee Galen | TEDxWoodLaneWomen
description:
In this insightful TEDx talk on mindful beauty, Dee Galen challenges the way we choose our skincare and beauty products, and why most of us are getting it wrong.
Drawing on nearly 30 years in the beauty industry, from manufacturing floors to brand development, Dee introduces her Three A's framework, a simple but transformative approach to taking back control of what you put on your skin:
1. Assess over assume – Stop buying on impulse and start understanding what your skin actually needs. 2. Align over follow – Look beyond the trending hero ingredients and find brands that truly share your values,  from sustainability to what's hiding in the 85–95% of a formulation nobody talks about. 3. Action over overwhelm – Use the tools now available to us, including AI, to cut through the marketing noise and make choices that fit your needs, your values, and your budget
Her talk is a wake-up call for anyone spending money on beauty without asking the deeper questions. In a £58 billion industry built on hype and highlight ingredients, Dee empowers consumers to stop chasing trends and start making mindful, meaningful choices for their skin and their wellbeing. If you've ever stood in a beauty aisle feeling overwhelmed and unsure, this talk is for you. Leading the way in brand and product development, clarifying brand positioning and
delivering above and beyond specific brand consumer needs, Dee has over 28 years
immersed in the beauty sector. Focused on luxury, efficacious products and brands, having worked both in-house and as a consultant to some of the most respected Skincare, Haircare, Wellbeing and Spa houses…Omorovicza, Aromatherapy Associates, Sarah Chapman, Elemis, QMS Medicosmetics, Philip Kingsley, This Works, Mandarin Oriental, Armani Spa, to name a few.

title: Why is President Trump trying to restrict what journalists can say? | BBC Americast

A major row has erupted between the US defense department and the journalists that cover its work after a memo was issued last month requiring journalists to accept a new set of reporting restrictions or face being barred from America’s military headquarters.

Suresh Konduru works in the field of enterprise transformation with a focus on agile practices and the use of artificial intelligence in organizational systems. He has several decades of experience working with large and complex organizations, supporting teams and leaders through change initiatives related to agility, learning, and adaptive ways of working.

title: What are forever chemicals, and how do they impact our health? | BBC News
description:
BBC reporter Catrin Nye has been carrying out an investigation for BBC Panorama into how so-called forever chemicals could affect people’s health and contaminate the environment.
 
Forever chemicals, or PFAS (per-and poly fluoroalkyl substances), are a group of about 10,000 chemicals and are used in anything from cookware, to waterproof clothes, electronics and medical equipment.
 
They are persistent pollutants, meaning they don't degrade easily and instead build up in the environment.
 
Scientists have linked a small number of them to serious harms, such as infertility and cancer.

The protests, which have reportedly spread to 180 cities and towns in all 31 provinces, were sparked by anger over the collapse of the Iranian currency and soaring cost of living. title: More Than Just a Flight: Inside the World of Aviation | Akya Bhatnagar | TEDxIIMCalcutta
description:
Why does an industry that moves millions of people every day struggle to make money and why does it still matter so deeply? In this talk, the speaker takes the audience inside the fascinating economics of the aviation industry, breaking down the real cost of flying from fuel and aircraft leases to crew, maintenance, and airport charges. Using simple numbers and relatable examples, the talk explains why airline margins are razor-thin and why a single discounted ticket can turn a profitable flight into a loss. But beyond the numbers lies a story of opportunity. With less than 10% of Indians having ever flown and India’s aviation capacity far below that of developed economies, the sector stands at the cusp of massive growth. The speaker explores how airlines are responding by investing in safety, personalization, digital innovation, operational efficiency, and sustainability to serve not just passengers, but aspirations. Drawing from personal experience working in aviation during the COVID-19 crisis, the talk also sheds light on what a modern aviation career looks like. From finance and operations to digital transformation and data analytics, the speaker illustrates how aviation offers diverse career paths and how a “T-shaped” skillset can help professionals grow across functions. At its heart, this talk reframes aviation as more than an industry it is a service that connects people, enables first-time flyers, supports families, and carries dreams across the sky. A compelling reminder that even in the toughest conditions, industries built on service, optimism, and resilience continue to help the world move forward. Akya Bhatnagar is an Indian professional whose profile indicates a background in electronics engineering, followed by a transition into audit analytics as part of Deloitte. 
 He has written on topics such as workplace fulfilment and meaning in work. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

title: Europe warns Trump of “dangerous downward spiral” and threatens tariff retaliation | BBC News
description:
European leaders have united in condemning President Trump’s threat of new tariffs against allies who oppose his plan to annexe  Greenland.    

A joint statement of European leaders said:  “Tariff threats undermine transatlantic relations and risk a dangerous downward spiral”.  The statement, signed by the leaders of Denmark, Norway, Sweden, France, Germany, the UK, the Netherlands and Finland said: “We are committed to upholding our sovereignty.” 

The UK Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer told the US president in a phone call that he was wrong to make such a threat against NATO allies.    

The EU made clear it could impose retaliatory tariffs on American goods or even consider economic sanctions against the United States if the US tariffs were imposed.  The head of the European Council announced an emergency summit and said  the EU showed “readiness to defend ourselves against any form of coercion”.

Europe’s stance could place it on a collision course with the US.  Trump has said he will place sanctions on eight European nations, including the UK, that have deployed troops to Greenland in response to US threats over its future.

Jane Hill presents BBC News at Ten reporting by Nick Beake, Joe Pike, Faisal Islam and Katya Adler.

title: Donald Trump’s claims about Nato troops in Afghanistan criticised | BBC News
description:
Donald Trump's claim that Nato troops stayed "a little off the front lines" during the war in Afghanistan has sparked outrage from UK politicians and veterans' families.
 
The US president told Fox News on Thursday that he was "not sure" the military alliance would be there for the US "if we ever needed them".
 
"They'll say they sent some troops to Afghanistan," he said, "and they did, they stayed a little back, a little off the front lines".
 
Health and Social Care Minister Stephen Kinnock called Trump’s remark “disappointing”, and said the UK and other allies had "always stood shoulder to shoulder with the United States" and contributed to US-led missions.
 
The UK was among several allies to join the US in Afghanistan from 2001, after it invoked Nato's collective security clause following the 9/11 terror attacks.
 
A total of 457 British service personnel were killed in the conflict.

title: The invisible suitcase | Daphne Kobia | TEDxEHLLausanne
description:
What does it mean to belong everywhere and nowhere? In this talk, Daphné unpacks the “invisible suitcase” she has dragged through 9 countries in 22 years, not filled with clothes, but with labels, masks, and performances. From Congo to Myanmar, from Belgium to Singapore, she reveals how identity is never halves or fractions, but a constellation of all we carry. Daphné Kobia is a student at EHL Hospitality Business School with a strong interest in innovation, branding, and cross-cultural communication. Alongside her studies, she is involved in Marketing and Communications at the EHL Innovation Hub, where she contributes to storytelling, positioning, and creative initiatives at the intersection of hospitality, entrepreneurship, and innovation.
She is also engaged in the broader EHL ecosystem through leadership, events, and ambassadorial roles, including work connected to luxury and brand environments. Daphné brings a globally informed perspective shaped by extensive international exposure, paired with a thoughtful, articulate approach to people, identity, and ideas.
Curious, observant, and highly adaptable, she combines strategic thinking with emotional intelligence, making her equally comfortable in creative, analytical, and multicultural settings. title: Who is Zohran Mamdani, frontrunner for New York City mayor? | BBC Americast
description:
Voting starts on Saturday for one of America’s biggest and most prominent political positions. 

How did Zohran Mamdani, the Democratic nominee, emerge as the frontrunner to be the next mayor of New York, despite being virtually unknown at the start of his campaign?   

Sarah, Justin and Anthony look in more detail at his policies, and in particular the centrepiece of his campaign around the cost of living. Mamdani says he will make New York more affordable, by increasing housing stock, raising taxes for the rich and bringing down the cost of rent. How realistic are his promises and how much could it matter if he can’t deliver? We also unpack his views on Israel and Gaza, and how his views on Gaza could affect the Jewish vote in New York, the biggest outside of Israel.   

We get an inside track on Mamdani’s campaign from Eric Lach, staff writer at the New Yorker, who has been following him on the campaign trail, from before he won the primaries, to having dinner at Mamdani’s apartment in Queens. He also shares his views on how Mamdani will handle the NYPD, the country’s largest police department, after calling for the police to be defunded in 2020.  

Donald Trump has made clear he thinks Mamdani is a radical left communist, so how might he handle the US president if he is elected as mayor? And how might Donald Trump target New York in return?

title: Trump warns Iran “massive armada” on way and time running out for nuclear deal | BBC News
description:
Donald Trump has warned Iran that "time is running out" to negotiate a deal on its nuclear programme following the build-up of US military forces in the Gulf.

The US president said a "massive Armada" was "moving quickly, with great power, enthusiasm, and purpose" towards Iran, referring to a large US naval fleet.

In response, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the country's armed forces were ready "with their fingers on the trigger" to "immediately and powerfully respond" to any aggression by land or sea.

Iran insists its nuclear programme is entirely peaceful and has repeatedly denied accusations by the US and its allies that it is seeking to develop nuclear weapons.

Trump's latest warning follows his promise that Washington would intervene to help those involved in the brutal and unprecedented crackdown on protests in the country earlier this month.

The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) says it has confirmed the killing of more than 6,301 people, including 5,925 protesters, since the unrest began at the end of December.  HRANA says it is also investigating another 17,000 reported deaths received despite an internet shutdown after nearly three weeks.  

Another group, the Norway-based Iran Human Rights (IHR), has warned that the final toll could exceed 25,000.

title: Several countries boycott Eurovision after Israel allowed to compete | BBC
description:
Ireland, Spain and the Netherlands will boycott next year's Eurovision Song Contest after it was decided Israel could compete. 

They were among a number of countries who had called for Israel to be excluded over the humanitarian toll of the war in Gaza, and accusations of unfair voting practices. 

Despite calls for a vote on Israel's participation, European Broadcasting Union (EBU) members voted on a package of measures at its biannual general meeting. 

The meeting also addressed new rules to limit the influence of governments on the results.

title: China hits growth goal after exports defy US tariffs | BBC News
description:
China said its economy expanded by 5% last year, meeting Beijing's official target as a record trade surplus boosted growth.
 
The world's second-largest economy reached its goal despite growth slowing to 4.5% in the final three months of 2025.
 
China's past year has been marked by struggles to boost domestic spending, a prolonged property crisis and turmoil caused by US President Donald Trump's tariff policies.
 
Experts said the figures point to a "two-speed economy", with manufacturing and exports propping up expansion while people are still spending cautiously and the real estate market continues to weigh on the country.

title: Life-changing eye implant helps blind patients read again | BBC News
description:
A group of blind patients can now read again after being fitted with a life-changing implant at the back of the eye.
 
A surgeon who inserted the microchips in five patients at Moorfields Eye Hospital in London says the results of the international trial are "astounding".
 
Sheila Irvine, 70, who is registered blind, told the BBC it was "out of this world" to be able to read and do crosswords again. 
 
The technology offers hope to people with an advanced form of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), called geographic atrophy (GA), which affects more than 250,000 people in the UK and five million worldwide.

title: How society thrives when we elevate mothers | Sahar Jamal | TEDxNairobi
description:
Women’s reproductive capacity is often treated as an inconvenient necessity at best—something to accommodate and tolerate. In truth, the hormones released throughout a woman’s reproductive journey unlock our core strengths. Not only do women have the capacity to birth human life, mothers also hold the key to our global economic prosperity and the wellbeing of our future generations. This talk explores how society can thrive when we elevate the alchemy of motherhood and recognize the leadership potential of women, not in spite of our biology, but because of it.

As founder of Maziwa, she is dedicated to ensuring Kenyan mothers never have to choose between breastfeeding and earning a living. Maziwa’s breast pumps, co-created with hundreds of Kenyan mothers, enable women to express milk discreetly in any work environment, while its Community Breastfeeding Ambassador program democratizes access to lactation support in underserved communities.

title: Russia hits Ukraine with rarely-used Oreshnik missile in fresh strikes | BBC News
description:
Russia has used the Oreshnik ballistic missile as part of a massive overnight strike on Ukraine.
 
At least four people were killed and 25 others injured in Kyiv on Thursday night, where loud booms could be heard for several hours, setting the sky alight with explosions.
 
It is only the second time that Moscow has used the Oreshnik, which was first deployed to hit the central city of Dnipro in November 2024.
 
It's an intermediate-range, hypersonic ballistic missile, meaning it can potentially reach up to 5,500km (3,417 miles).
 
Russia's defence ministry said the strike was a response to a Ukrainian drone attack on Vladimir Putin's residence in late December, which Kyiv denies carrying out.

title: How K-beauty went from viral trend to economic powerhouse | BBC News
description:
K-beauty is one of the biggest industries in South Korea, where the pressure to look almost flawless has always been huge in a highly competitive society.

In the first half of 2025, South Korea overtook France, the birthplace of modern cosmetics, to become the world's second-largest exporter of beauty products, after the United States.

Social media has been central to this shift. Products launched in Seoul are on TikTok and Instagram feeds in the US, UK, India and Australia instantly.

There are however growing concerns about the social impact of beauty ideals, particularly on young people. Experts warn that constant exposure to skincare content online can fuel anxiety and excessive spending.

title: EU set to scrap 2035 petrol and diesel car ban | BBC News
description:
The EU has confirmed it will water down its landmark 2035 ban on the sale of new petrol and diesel cars.

The decision came after lobbying by carmakers and several EU leaders.

Under current legislation, manufacturers were forced to ensure that 100% of cars and van production had zero emissions up to 2035.

The European Commission is now confirming this will be reduced to 90%, allowing the manufacturer of hybrid electric cars and combustion engines beyond 2035.

Seen by some as a victory for the European car industry, the Green party in the European parliament have been quick to denounce the decision.

During the ban, which lasted until the year 2000, those who were gay - or were perceived to be - faced intrusive investigations, dismissal and in some cases imprisonment.

title: Every Word Leaves a Trace | Jayshree Kirtane | TEDxBIT Jaipur
description:
In a world where conversations move fast and opinions move faster, we often underestimate the quiet power of our words. But what if every sentence we speak leaves an invisible imprint — on someone’s mind, heart, or future? In this deeply reflective and thought-provoking talk at TEDxBITJaipur, Jayshree Kirtane explores how language is not just communication — it is creation. Every word carries energy. Through relatable stories and real-life experiences, she reminds us that words are never “just words.” They become memories. They become beliefs. They become the inner voice someone carries long after the conversation ends. This talk is a powerful reminder to pause before we speak, to choose empathy over impulse, and to recognize the responsibility that comes with expression. Because sometimes, a single sentence can change someone’s entire story.
 Jayshree (JK) brings over 30 years of experience spanning academia, coaching, and leadership development. Beginning her career as a professor of quantitative subjects in management schools, a serendipitous coaching encounter two decades ago led her to transition from Mathematical Economics to Applied Psychology. title: Migrant sex offender given £500 after threat to disrupt deportation | BBC News
description:
A migrant sex offender who was mistakenly released from prison was given a £500 payment after threatening to disrupt his deportation from the UK to Ethiopia, the BBC understands.
 
Hadush Kebatu was jailed after sexually assaulting a 14-year-old girl and a woman while living in an asylum hotel in Epping, Essex, but was mistakenly set free by prison staff on Friday and was brought back into custody following a two-day manhunt.
 
It is understood the payment was a decision made by the removal team, not ministers, and was considered as an alternative to a more expensive process.
 
Kebatu was not on the government's Facilitated Returns Scheme - for foreign national offenders who agree to leave the UK voluntarily - under which he would have been given £1,500.

title: Palestine Action wins High Court challenge against government ban | BBC News
description:
The High Court has ruled that the ban of Palestine Action under terrorism legislation is unlawful - but it remains in place for now.

Three senior judges said that while Palestine Action use criminality to promote its aims, its activities had not crossed the very high bar to make it a terrorist organisation.

The judges however rule the ban must remain until another hearing on 20 February on what happens next.

The Met Police said it will continue to identify offences where support for Palestine Action is being shown, but will focus on gathering evidence rather than making arrests.

The UK government said it will appeal the decision, with Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood saying she's "disappointed”.

Palestine Action's co-founder Huda Ammori called the ruling a "monumental victory for both our fundamental freedoms in Britain and in the struggle for freedom for the Palestinian people”.
